summary: Describes an LDAP version 3 control that returns only the attribute values matching a filter, instead of every value of an attribute. Without it, a client must fetch all values and search through them itself.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of getting the whole toy box and sorting it yourself, you ask for only the red toys.

questions: return only matching attribute values in ldap
what is the ldap matched values control
how to return only some attribute values in ldap
subtitle: An LDAP control that returns only the attribute values you asked for, not every value stored.

tldr.problem: When a client reads an LDAPv3 attribute, it can normally get either just the attribute type or all of its values. An attribute with many values, such as userCertificate, forces the client to download everything and filter locally.
tldr.mechanism: The valuesReturnFilter control carries a list of simple filter items with a Search request. The server returns only the attribute values that evaluate TRUE against at least one item.
tldr.outcome: Clients no longer need to implement matching rules or process irrelevant values. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and registers the control under OID 1.2.826.0.1.3344810.2.3.

facts.label: Filter item types
facts.value: 7 (equality, substrings, greater or equal, less or equal, present, approx, extensible)

today: RFC 3876 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Problem With All-or-Nothing Attributes
sections.content:
In LDAPv3 (see RFC 2251), reading an attribute from an entry normally gives you the attribute type alone, or the type with all of its values. There is no way to ask for just a few values.

That hurts when an attribute holds many values, such as userCertificate, or the subschema attributes objectClasses and attributeTypes. Without this control the client must read every value and filter locally, which means it has to implement the matching rules itself and process many irrelevant values. That is inefficient when values are large or complex.

This RFC defines a control that returns only values that matched (returned TRUE to) one or more elements of a newly defined values return filter. It is especially useful with extensible matching rules that match on parts of complex binary values.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a drawer with hundreds of keys, and you can only take the whole drawer home. This control lets you say which keys you want and take only those.

sections.title: How the Control Behaves
sections.content:
The valuesReturnFilter control only has meaning for the Search operation, and a client SHOULD only add it to Search. It may be critical or non-critical, as the user decides. If the server supports it and it is present on a Search, the server MUST obey it whatever the criticality flag says.

If the control is critical and the server does not support it, or it is applied to something other than Search, the server MUST return unavailableCriticalExtension. If it is non-critical in those cases, the server MUST ignore it.

When the server uses the control, it works in steps:

  • The Search filter runs first to find the matching entries. The control has no impact on this step.
  • If typesOnly is TRUE, or the requested attributes are only the OID 1.1 (no attributes), the control has no effect.
  • For each requested attribute of each matching entry, a value that evaluates TRUE against one or more filter elements is returned. A value that evaluates FALSE or undefined against all elements is left out. An attribute with no values selected is returned with an empty set of values.

If the attribute list is empty or an asterisk, the control applies to every user attribute. If it contains a plus sign, the control applies to every operational attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: First the librarian finds the right books. Then, instead of handing over every page, she gives you only the pages that match your note. If no page matches, you get an empty folder.

sections.title: The Control Value
sections.content:
The control's OID is 1.2.826.0.1.3344810.2.3. Its controlValue is an OCTET STRING holding the BER encoding of an ASN.1 value of type ValuesReturnFilter, which is a SEQUENCE OF SimpleFilterItem.

A SimpleFilterItem is a choice of equalityMatch, substrings, greaterOrEqual, lessOrEqual, present, approxMatch or extensibleMatch. These look like the item types in an ordinary LDAP search filter, but there are no AND, OR or NOT operators: the list is simply a set of alternatives, and a value is returned if it satisfies any of them.

The extensibleMatch item uses a SimpleMatchingAssertion, with an optional matchingRule, an optional type (at least one of the two must be present) and a required matchValue. All the data types have their standard meanings from the LDAPv3 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The note you hand over is a short list of things to look for. Any page that matches anything on the list is kept.

sections.title: X.500 Roots and Other Controls
sections.content:
The control is a superset of the matchedValuesOnly (MVO) boolean in the X.500 Directory Access Protocol Search argument. The LDAP Extensions working group found ambiguities in the MVO boolean, for example whether it governed only values that contributed to the truth of the filter or all values. It chose a simple filter that removes any doubt about whether a value is selected.

Values discarded by this control MUST NOT be reinstated by other controls. The control acts independently of controls such as server side sorting (RFC 2891), but the order of controls in the request can change the results. If sorting runs first and value filtering second, results may look misordered because the sort key values were removed. If entry duplication runs first, there may be identical duplicate entries with empty attribute value sets.

For these reasons the ValuesReturnFilter control in a SearchRequest SHOULD precede other controls that affect the number and ordering of SearchResultEntrys.
sections.plainLanguage: If you sort your cards and then throw some away, the pile may look out of order. So the throwing-away step should come first.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a string form for filters using ABNF, for example ((mail=*hotmail.com)(telephoneNumber=*)), and three examples in LDIF.

  • Mixed attributes: a search for (sn=mullan) asking for mail,telephoneNumber with that control returns the one matching mail value ending in hotmail.com and all telephoneNumber values, because telephoneNumber=* matches everything.
  • Schema lookup: in a subschema subentry holding 35 attribute descriptions, the filter ((attributeTypes=1.2.3.4.5)) returns only the one description for the attribute named gunk.
  • Certificates: with the filter ((userCertificate=1357$o=truetrust ltd,c=gb)), only the certificate with serial number 1357 from that issuer is returned. This needs a server that supports the certificateExactMatch matching rule.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask a phone book for one person's email but all of their phone numbers, or ask a huge catalogue for one single item.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not primarily discuss security. It does require that attribute values are returned only if the server's access controls allow it, so the control has no effect on what a client is permitted to see.

It notes the control may help public key infrastructure deployment: searching for specific certificates becomes more scalable and practical, since the client avoids downloading many irrelevant certificates.

The control is registered as the Matched Values control, with Specification RFC3876 and the OID 1.2.826.0.1.3344810.2.3, which TrueTrust Ltd assigned under its British Standards Institution registered company number.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules about who may see what still apply. This control only narrows down what you get, it never lets you see more.

data.title: ValuesReturnFilter ASN.1
data.code:
ValuesReturnFilter ::= SEQUENCE OF SimpleFilterItem

SimpleFilterItem ::= CHOICE {
        equalityMatch   [3] AttributeValueAssertion,
        substrings      [4] SubstringFilter,
        greaterOrEqual  [5] AttributeValueAssertion,
        lessOrEqual     [6] AttributeValueAssertion,
        present         [7] AttributeDescription,
        approxMatch     [8] AttributeValueAssertion,
        extensibleMatch [9] SimpleMatchingAssertion }
